newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina's Menem resorts to kinder, gentler style.
newsitem.headline: Argentina's Menem resorts to kinder, gentler style.

text.p: Dogged by plummeting public approval ratings, Argentine President Carlos Menem has had to moderate his bulldozer style and pay closer attention to the demands of his own Peronist Party legislators.

"Menem's leadership resembles more and more that of Brazilian President (Fernando Henrique) Cardoso and less and less that of Peruvian President (Alberto) Fujimori," leading political analyst Rosendo Fraga told Reuters.
Fraga was referring to the ease with which Fujimori moves his initiatives through the Peruvian Congress, in stark contrast with the hard bargaining that Cardoso faces from his own ruling coalition.
The reason for the weakening of Menem's power and the growing lack of discipline within his party is a consequence of the lost luster of his economic policies, analysts say.
With the country only slowly emerging from a yearlong recession and unemployment at 17 percent, Argentines are showing growing signs of impatience with the government's economic austerity recipes.

The Peronists, with a long tradition of populism, have begun to worry that under this harsher new reality they will no longer be able to win national and mid-term votes as they consistently did since Menem's advent to power in 1989.

Analysts also point out that with Menem well into his second term and no possibilities of running again in 1999, the loyalty of his once closest allies is flailing, as they look for fresh power options.

"It's quite simple. As time goes by, Menem loses power and has to look for a different, more conciliatory style," said analyst Daniel Rodriguez Lamas. "His challenge now is how to lead the country knowing his days are numbered."
Menem recently fired his once flamboyant and powerful Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo and replaced him with the self-effacing Central Bank President Roque Fernandez.
He took over the responsibility of rallying support for his new minister's austerity package, needed to reduce a growing fiscal deficit.

With that in mind, Menem invited to the presidential residence the party's top brass and begged them for support. Still, days later Fernandez's watered-down economic package failed to move through Congress, where Menem has a majority in both houses.
"There is a great erosion (of power)," said leading financial consultant Miguel Angel Broda.

During his first years in office, the Menem-Cavallo duo zoomed past Congress with key reforms. When lawmakers dragged their feet, Menem resorted to presidential decrees. A dismembered opposition was no challenge to his aggressive style.
Menem privatised state firms and changed economic rules, throwing the country open to foreign competition.
Taming runaway inflation and sparking strong growth, his reforms won him worldwide acclaim and a reelection in 1995 with a 50 percent margin.
But analysts winced at his style which they said sometimes showed outright contempt for democratic procedures.
They cited as examples his forcing a close associate of his as Supreme Court chief and bypassing Congress with an overdose of presidential decrees to implement key legislation.

In stark contrast, some days ago Menem offered his allies in Congress to meet regularly and pledged to maintain "a new form of relationship between the government and lawmakers...to analyse with absolute sincerity the country's problems."
Analyst Broda pointed out that those are signs which ultimately show the country will have more "real democracy."
But he also said there were two sides to the coin, wondering if key laws needed to continue with Argentina's reforms will ever move forward if they have to negotiate the myriad corridors of Congress.
"This political habitat will certainly limit future reforms," said Broda.
